extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatherists, literary critics, and informed theatre audiences
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical standards for evaluating/constructing stage plays (characterization, dramatic probability, moral purpose, staging, and causal coherence). Geared toward assessing tragedies and sensational/melodramatic drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character desirability vs. vice
rubrics_metrics.description: “Meantime the qualities of his character are too desirable, too flattering to our pride and our wishes, not to make up on this side as much additional faith as was lost on the other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character is made overly attractive or flattering, audiences will be inclined to excuse or rationalize their vices; avoid crafting protagonists whose good qualities swamp their faults in ways that undermine moral and dramatic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of mind / intellectual superiority as dramatic engine
rubrics_metrics.description: “But of all power, that of the mind is, on every account, the grand desideratum of human ambition... the coexistence of great intellectual lordship with guilt has never been adequately represented without exciting the strongest interest.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting characters intellectual power (and especially fearless superiority to invisible fears) creates strong dramatic interest — the combination of intellect and moral failing is particularly compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability achieved through harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: “On this propensity... a specific dramatic probability may be raised by a true poet, if the whole of his work be in harmony: a dramatic probability, sufficient for dramatic pleasure, even when the component characters and incidents border on impossibility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play need not be literally probable so long as the whole work is internally harmonious; coherence across tone, character, and incident permits audiences to 'yield themselves to a dream' and accept improbabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character to the end
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘tremendous consistency with which he stands out the last fearful trial, like a second Prometheus.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained, consistent behavior — even to final extremities — produces sublimity; abrupt departures from established character reduce dramatic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of character traits (mixing 'ingredients')
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ingredients too are mixed in the happiest proportion, so as to uphold and relieve each other—more especially in that constant interpoise of wit, gaiety, and social generosity, which prevents the criminal... from sinking into the mere ruffian.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine contrasting traits (wit, gaiety, generosity) with darker traits to keep characters complex and maintain audience interest; avoid one-dimensional villainy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of manners and breeding to vivify drama
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fine suffusion through the whole, with the characteristic manners and feelings, of a highly bred gentleman gives life to the drama.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social manners and refined comportment can animate character and lend plausibility and interest; incorporate these consistently to enrich the stage picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose behind spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nor is the scene... interesting, in dramatic probability alone; it is susceptible likewise of a sound moral... presents them for the sole purpose of displaying their hollowness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular or showy qualities should serve a moral or critical purpose; dramatize to illuminate or critique, not merely to titillate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subversion of natural causes and effects for surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: “The whole secret of the modern jacobinical drama... consists in the confusion and subversion of the natural order of things in their causes and effects... rewarding with all the sympathies... those criminals...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manufacture surprise by reversing cause and effect or by rewarding vice unearned; maintain causal order so sympathy and judgment remain intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground supernatural effects; give consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is a mere supernatural effect, without even a hint of any supernatural agency; a prodigy, without any circumstance mentioned that is prodigious; and a miracle introduced without a ground, and ending without a result.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using supernatural or miraculous elements, provide narrative grounding and show consequences; gratuitous prodigies undermine dramatic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of scenes — avoid 'a scene for the sake of a scene'
rubrics_metrics.description: “A scene for the sake of a scene, without a word spoken; as such, therefore, (a rarity without a precedent), we must take it, and be thankful!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each scene should justify its presence by contributing to character, plot, theme, or mood; avoid inserting spectacle that lacks narrative purpose unless deliberately offered as gratuitous spectacle and acknowledged as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausible character speech and desires
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Imogine asking a painter to paint 'The thoughts, the recollections, sweet and bitter, Or the Elysian dreams of lovers' — requests 'that have neither lines nor colours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue and expressed desires should be rooted in believable psychology and circumstance; avoid unreal or absurd requests that strain plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive, puppet-like secondary characters
rubrics_metrics.description: “Clotilda... very much reminds us of those puppet-heroines, for whom the showman contrives to dialogue without any skill in ventriloquism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting characters should have agency and natural speech; avoid creating passive foils who exist only to elicit exposition or affirm the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle retrospective narration carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The play 'tells well and passionately the preliminary circumstances, and thus overcomes the main difficulty of most first acts, to wit, that of retrospective narration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find effective, dramatic ways to convey backstory in early acts (showing, scenes, credible confessions) rather than relying on clumsy exposition; when used, ensure diction and metre are controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of character and appropriate responsive action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prior 'does nothing but scold' though he knows Bertram's gang are assassins; author preserves a scolding Prior who never takes suitable action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should act in ways consistent with their knowledge, duties, and stakes (e.g., a Prior who knows of danger ought to take credible protective action), or be given motives that explain inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain improbable survivals and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: The rescue/survival of Bertram's gang is presented without explanation leaving readers to conjecture how all were saved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t leave crucial causal gaps (e.g., mass survival, sudden rescues) unexplained; provide plausible mechanics or acceptably poetic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrived madness used solely for stage effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical 'madness' is described as 'a sort of intermittent fever with fits of lightheadedness... whenever occasion and stage effect happen to call for it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological states portrayed onstage should be motivated and consistent with character and plot, not toggled purely to produce stage effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichéd, vague, and borrowed descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of phrases like 'wild and terrible dark eyes' and other 'common-place indefinites' often copied from other writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fresh, precise, and character-specific descriptions instead of stock epithets or slavish imitation of other authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid formulaic melodramatic gestures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence of raving, yelling, fainting, relenting, curtain drop described as mechanical 'series of super-tragic starts, pauses, screams, struggling, dagger-throwing...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of mechanical staging that repeats familiar melodramatic beats without psychological cause; make emotional arcs earned and varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect audience moral sensibilities; don't pander to outrages
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes public appetite for the 'grossest and most outrageous stimulants' and audience applause for shocking, indecent representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of how sensational content may desensitize or pander to base appetites; consider moral effect and purpose when staging shocking material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage spectacle should serve narrative, not merely fill sight-hungry audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: chorister boys singing on the altar; mute dramatis personae moving simply 'to afford something to be seen' for audience members who cannot hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual or musical spectacle must have dramatic justification; avoid adding extras or tableaux purely to entertain inattentive viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incoherent, derivative lines and voice breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Imogine’s two lines are called 'senseless plagiarism' lifted from Lear and Dryden and standing unique and incongruent in her speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain voice consistency and originality; don’t insert borrowed lines that clash with a character’s established diction or break dramatic cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sudden, unexplained reversals in character behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prior's sudden revolution from scolding to whining, weeping, and kneeling is described as 'surprising' and 'outré.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major shifts in temperament or stance must be foreshadowed or motivated; abrupt reversals confuse and alienate audiences unless intentionally presented and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal coherence and proportionality of antecedents and consequents
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Conclusion: 'The sense of Before and After becomes both intelligible and intellectual when... we contemplate the succession in the relations of Cause and Effect... The sense of proportion between antecedents and consequents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure events follow intelligible causal lines and that consequences are proportionate to antecedents; audiences take comfort in perceivable causation and intelligibility of outcomes.
